analysis.one_liner: Ends the federal permission that lets states ban agreements requiring workers to join or pay fees to a union.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on September 4, 2025, and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has sat with no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal labor law, about half of states have "right-to-work" laws that prohibit union contracts requiring employees to join a union or pay union fees. This bill repeals the section of federal law (Section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act) that gives states that power, which would allow unions in every state to negotiate contracts requiring all covered workers to pay for union representation. It has not received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in states with right-to-work laws would gain the most: unions would be able to negotiate contracts requiring everyone covered by a union contract to join or pay fees, strengthening union finances and bargaining power, which typically translates into better wages and workplace protections for union members.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and unions in right-to-work states

how_it_helps.text: By repealing Section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act, the bill ends the federal permission states rely on to ban union security agreements, so every state could require non-union workers to pay fees covering union bargaining costs.
Weaker union finances are associated with lower bargaining power; strengthening unions' ability to collect fees supports the wages and protections they negotiate for workers.

analysis.who_pays: Workers who prefer not to join a union would again owe union fees where their state permits mandatory fees; employers, particularly in right-to-work states, would face unions with stronger finances and greater organizing leverage.

drawbacks.text: Workers who do not want to join a union would again be subject to mandatory union fees in states that drop their right-to-work laws, which supporters of those laws frame as a forced-payment concern.
The bill would override the policy choices of the roughly half of states that have adopted right-to-work laws, which their governments argue help them attract employers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would be meaningful for workers seeking to organize in right-to-work states, and the cost—unions collecting fees from workers who choose not to join—is real but limited to that specific context. The bill has no path forward in a Senate where Republicans hold a majority and no Democratic cosponsor from a right-to-work state has signed on, so its drawbacks were never seriously weighed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and nothing has happened since.

narrative.text: The bill's only actions are its introduction on September 4, 2025, and its referral to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The committee has taken no further action, and the Senate has not voted on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost; employers in right-to-work states are better off only in the sense that the status quo, which bars mandatory union fees, continues untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No change yet; status quo continues

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal Section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act.

for.name: Bernie Sanders and 13 other Democratic senators (Duckworth, Padilla, Blumenthal, Gillibrand, Booker, Fetterman, Baldwin, Hirono, Klobuchar, Merkley, Markey, Smith, Welch)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 15 cosponsors are Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors are Democrats or an allied independent; no Republican or bipartisan support appears in the record.

industries.note: Unions could once again negotiate contracts requiring all covered employees to pay fees or join, strengthening their finances and bargaining position in right-to-work states.

industries.industry: Employers (especially low-wage and southern/manufacturing employers in right-to-work states)
industries.note: Employers in right-to-work states would face unions with more financial security and stronger ability to organize their workplaces, raising the prospect of higher labor costs.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and referral to the HELP Committee with no hearing or markup scheduled, the bill is very unlikely to advance in this Congress; bills referred to committee without action typically die there.
